Construction of housing units required by population increases will result in losses of land for other uses. Because most of the induced increase is expected to occur in Hardin, irrigated land in the Big Horn Valley adjacent to Hardin will be converted to residential use as the town expands.
Approximately 45% of Tract II and 24% of Tract III is covered with a Ponderosa pine stand estimated to average 3300 board feet to the acre. This would be removed ahead of the mining operation. It is unknown whether the area can be reforested. Timber production in this area is at best a marginal operation, and mining will eliminate much of the environment needed for timber growth.
Mining will alter the surface water system which now exists and the ground water will be altered to the depth of the Robinson coal seam.
There are approximately 90 springs on and adjacent to Tracts II and III. The loss of some of these springs is probable; this will represent a serious loss to local cattlemen. It may be possible to drill for water, or surface water impoundments may be necessary if cattle are to use the area again. If a stable water supply cannot be developed, dryland farming may be the only use which could be made of the land. It may prove feasible to farm much more of the area, as the reclaimed land will be much smoother than now exists.
